summary_plain: This ground investigation used computational modeling to study how heat and gas flow affect cool flames around burning fuel droplets in microgravity. Researchers simulated n-alkane and oxygenated fuel droplets under various ambient conditions to map when cool flames ignite, oscillate, or go out. Understanding these dynamics helps improve spacecraft fire safety and design better detection and prevention systems.
summary_expert: The study developed a 3-D OpenFOAM CFD model coupling variable-density Navier-Stokes flow, low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation to analyze n-alkane and butanol droplet combustion in microgravity. Simulations examined three forcing modes—convection alone to mimic droplet drift, imposed heat flux, and combined convection plus heating—across large and sub-millimeter droplets under varying ambient compositions (including ozone-assisted cases) and pressures. Model fidelity was evaluated against ISS FLEX measurements and droplet diameter regression data, generating stability maps for cool-flame onset, persistence, oscillation, and extinction.

key_findings.text: The initial ignition source energy variation has negligible influence on the quasi-steady droplet burning, only minimally affecting the initial ignition transient.

key_findings.text: The droplet regression rate decreases with increasing xenon content for a fixed droplet diameter contributing reductions in burning rate and earlier flame extinction at larger extinction diameters.

key_findings.text: An increase in xenon content diminishes both the maximum peak gas temperature and maximum rate of increase of the peak gas temperature.

key_findings.text: The flame stand-off ratio is found to be weakly dependent on the initial droplet sizes while it is strongly affected by the ambient gas composition.

source.file: documents/PSI-117/PSI-117_Reports_Dissertation_Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N-Alka.pdf

key_findings.text: The limiting oxygen index for xenon was found to be approximately 4%, 5% and 6% for 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm droplet sizes respectively, while comparative analysis revealed limiting oxygen index values of 5%, 8%, 21% and 21% for xenon, argon, helium and carbon dioxide respectively for an initial drop diameter of 1.5 mm.
